implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines supplies the coordination the language itself does not: coroutineScope is the master's structured lifetime (it waits for children, propagates exceptions and cancels siblings), async is dispatch, awaitAll is the join, and the coroutine context decides placement - Dispatchers.Default for CPU work on a shared bounded pool, Dispatchers.IO for blocking calls, or limitedParallelism(n) to pin a view of a dispatcher to n threads instead of creating a pool per master. For a persistent worker set with dynamic balancing, model the work pool as a Channel and launch N workers that range over it (fan-out), then close the channel to end the loops. Because one child's failure cancels the whole scope, a single failing sub-task aborts its siblings - use supervisorScope or catch per child when partial results are wanted.
pitfalls: One failing child cancels the scope and every sibling sub-task unless supervisorScope or a per-child try/catch is used.
Blocking calls on Dispatchers.Default starve the shared pool; use Dispatchers.IO, runInterruptible, or a dedicated limitedParallelism dispatcher.
Structured concurrency only holds inside a scope: async on GlobalScope or a throwaway Job escapes the join and leaks work.
Cancellation is cooperative - code that ignores isActive (busy loops, blocking calls) keeps running after the scope is cancelled.
